description: This working paper develops a measurement framework for comparing AI infrastructure investment and economic-resilience context across ten economies. It argues that AI infrastructure financing cannot be assessed through headline investment totals alone because records differ in realization status, AI specificity, accounting basis, capital-formation eligibility, national coverage, and deployment timing. The study compares financing architectures in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Germany, France, Singapore, China, and India, while treating AI-IIS, PAIIS, and PrAIIS as bounded measurement concepts rather than presently comparable national statistics. It concludes that meaningful cross-country investment comparison and later resilience testing require aligned scope, period matching, denominator completeness, and operational-capacity timing.
abstract: Countries are expanding AI infrastructure through markedly different combinations of public and private capital, yet cross-country assessment is complicated by inconsistent investment accounting, incomplete national coverage, and the lag between expenditure and usable capacity. This study compares financing architectures across ten economies: the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Germany, France, Singapore, China, and India. Public AI Infrastructure Investment Share (PAIIS), Private AI Infrastructure Investment Share (PrAIIS), and AI infrastructure investment intensity (AI-IIS) are treated as bounded measurement concepts rather than presently comparable national statistics. The analysis distinguishes source quality, realization status, AI specificity, accounting basis, capital-formation eligibility, and deployment timing. Qualifying AI-specific realized monetary records are available from five economies, but national coverage remains incomplete and several records combine capital and operating expenditure. France provides completed-project funding with unresolved payment timing; Germany and Singapore provide procurement evidence; China provides realized broader-compute CAPEX that is too broad for an AI-only numerator; and India reports mission-wide expenditure without an infrastructure-specific split. The study therefore compares financing architecture, monetary evidence, and deployment timing rather than constructing national investment rankings. Macroeconomic and labor-market indicators are reported only as descriptive context. The findings show that scope, accounting treatment, realization status, deployment timing, and coverage must be aligned before meaningful cross-country investment comparisons or subsequent resilience analysis can be undertaken.

methodology.framework_name: AI Infrastructure Financing, Deployment, and Resilience Measurement Framework
methodology.source_basis: Comparative cross-country analysis using official or first-party AI-infrastructure project, program, financing, operating, accounting, and macroeconomic sources, supplemented where necessary by documented procurement mirrors and harmonized macroeconomic/labor-market data.
methodology.case_context: Ten-economy comparison covering the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Germany, France, Singapore, China, and India, with monetary observations verified at the 19 August 2026 data freeze.
methodology.core_problem: The central measurement problem is that AI infrastructure investment records differ across announcements, commitments, procurement awards, subsidies, public accounts, company CAPEX, completed projects, mission expenditures, and operating programs, making headline cross-country investment totals misleading unless scope, status, timing, accounting, and denominator coverage are aligned.
central_claims: AI-IIS, PAIIS, and PrAIIS should be treated as bounded measurement concepts rather than presently comparable national statistics.
Public-private financing architecture is analytically distinct from investment scale.
Realized monetary evidence is not automatically capital formation because some records combine hardware, integration, operation, or unknown cost components.
Investment timing and usable AI-capacity activation must be coded separately because expenditure can precede service availability.
Descriptive macroeconomic and labor-market indicators are not direct resilience measures without a common shock, baseline, counterfactual, and recovery trajectory.
Meaningful cross-country comparison requires aligned scope, accounting treatment, realization status, deployment timing, and coverage.

analytical_lenses.name: Source-Quality Assessment
analytical_lenses.description: Distinguishes audited accounts, official project documentation, institutional records, company reports, procurement evidence, and secondary mirrors.

analytical_lenses.name: Realization-Status Classification
analytical_lenses.description: Separates realized expenditure, actual outturn, accepted or paid CAPEX, completed-project funding, procurement awards, budgets, commitments, announcements, and plans.

analytical_lenses.name: AI-Specificity Screen
analytical_lenses.description: Separates AI-specific infrastructure from mission-wide, broader-compute, mixed-use AI/HPC, or insufficiently attributed spending.

analytical_lenses.name: Accounting-Basis Classification
analytical_lenses.description: Distinguishes cash outturn, payment-basis CAPEX, acceptance-basis CAPEX, company-reported actual investment, incurred project cost, program execution, procurement awards, revised estimates, and mission-wide expenditure.

analytical_lenses.name: Capital-Formation Eligibility
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses whether monetary evidence is CAPEX-only, mixed CAPEX/OPEX, or unknown before treating it as a capital-investment numerator.

analytical_lenses.name: Deployment-Lag Coding
analytical_lenses.description: Separates expenditure and capital formation from service activation and operational availability.

analytical_lenses.name: Descriptive Outcome Context
analytical_lenses.description: Uses macroeconomic and labor-market composites only as sample-relative descriptive context rather than resilience rankings.

dimensions.name: AI Infrastructure Investment Intensity
dimensions.description: Qualifying AI-infrastructure investment relative to nominal GDP over a matched period.
dimensions.interpretation: Valid only when numerator and denominator periods match and the numerator is sufficiently complete, consistently scoped, and capital-eligible.

dimensions.name: Public AI Infrastructure Investment Share
dimensions.description: Public share of a defensible bounded AI-infrastructure financing pool.
dimensions.interpretation: Reported only when public and total denominators are known for a common project or program pool; not a national statistic when coverage is incomplete.

dimensions.name: Private AI Infrastructure Investment Share
dimensions.description: Private share of a defensible bounded AI-infrastructure financing pool.
dimensions.interpretation: Reported only when private and total denominators are known for a common project or program pool; unresolved residual financing is not mechanically assigned.

dimensions.name: Source Quality
dimensions.description: Reliability and specificity of monetary or institutional evidence.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Sources range from audited public accounts and annual reports to official documentation and procurement mirrors.
dimensions.interpretation: Evidence type must be preserved rather than merged into a single investment total.

dimensions.name: Realization Status
dimensions.description: Whether a record is realized expenditure, outturn, accepted or paid CAPEX, completed-project funding, procurement award, commitment, budget, or announcement.
dimensions.interpretation: Only realized or closely verified monetary records support realized spending analysis.

dimensions.name: AI Specificity
dimensions.description: Whether the record is AI-specific, mission-wide, broader-compute, mixed-use AI/HPC, or unknown.
dimensions.interpretation: Broader-compute and mission-wide records cannot be used as AI-only numerators without a defensible split.

dimensions.name: Capital-Formation Eligibility
dimensions.description: Whether the monetary amount represents CAPEX-only, mixed CAPEX/OPEX, or unknown cost composition.
dimensions.interpretation: Realized monetary evidence is not automatically realized capital formation.

dimensions.name: Operational Availability
dimensions.description: Whether capacity was available within the 2023–2025 outcome window or activated afterward.
dimensions.interpretation: Same-year expenditure is not same-year AI-capability exposure when service activation occurs later.

key_findings: The ten economies do not follow a single public-private AI-infrastructure financing model.
Qualifying AI-specific realized monetary records are available from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, and South Korea, but national coverage remains incomplete.

France provides completed-project funding with unresolved payment timing; Germany and Singapore provide procurement-award evidence; China provides realized broader-compute CAPEX that is too broad for an AI-only numerator; India reports mission-wide expenditure without an infrastructure-specific split.
Japan used subsidies and policy finance to leverage privately owned GPU-cloud capacity.
South Korea combined public GPU-program funding with private CSP hosting and operation, but the hardware-versus-integration-and-operating-cost split remained unresolved.
The United States relied primarily on private hyperscale capital with decentralized public incentives and enabling measures.
The United Kingdom combined private data-center build-out with publicly funded compute and strategic capacity.
Canada combined catalytic public support with private/host delivery for dedicated AI computing capacity.
Valid monetary records could not be interpreted automatically as same-period usable AI capacity because service activation often occurred after expenditure.
The descriptive outcome composites reveal macroeconomic and labor-market variation but should not be interpreted as resilience rankings.

No cross-country correlation coefficient was estimated because comparable realized monetary observations were small, national coverage differed, accounting bases were not harmonized, and contemporaneous capability exposure was insufficient.
AI-IIS, PAIIS, and PrAIIS cannot yet be constructed as comparable national statistics from the available records.
strategic_implications: AI-infrastructure strategy should be evaluated through qualifying monetary scale, allocation of cost and risk, conversion speed, access, strategic purpose, and post-shock outcomes rather than headline investment announcements alone.
Public-private financing shares should not be treated as evidence of complementarity without information on crowding-in, risk sharing, deployment, access, and conversion efficiency.
Announced investment with long deployment delays or narrow access should not be assumed to improve economic resilience.
Future resilience testing should use post-operational panels, matched investment periods, explicit coverage denominators, and shock-specific resistance and recovery metrics.

policy_recommendations: Separate announcements, commitments, procurement awards, budgets, completed-project funding, realized expenditure, and CAPEX before comparing AI-infrastructure investment across countries.
Report public and private financing shares only for bounded project or program pools with defensible denominators.
Track deployment timing and operational availability separately from spending and capital formation.
Avoid constructing national rankings when scope, accounting basis, realization status, and coverage are not harmonized.
Use descriptive macroeconomic and labor-market indicators only as context unless a common shock, baseline, and recovery trajectory are available.
Develop future post-operational datasets that align investment periods, operational capacity exposure, and resilience outcomes.
